title: Calorimetry (part 3)
textbookText: Newton’s law of cooling. [Fig. 11.2 (a), Soup in a bowl] Have you ever held a warm bowl full of food in your hand, and wondered why it seems to cool down rapidly at first but stays lukewarm for much longer? Also, the hot soup will be too hot to eat for the first few minutes, but eventually, it reaches a temperature we can enjoy it. Then we can eat the soup leisurely over some more minutes, and it stays warm for much longer. We may have a query that how fast a cup of boiling water will cool down in a kitchen at room temperature. In all of above activities, there is a relationship between temperature difference of hot substance with its surroundings and the time taken by it to cool down. Newton's law of cooling describes how fast a substance cools down. Also, it establishes a relationship between the temperature of a substance and the time taken by the substance to cool down. During cooling of hot liquid exposed to the surroundings of lower temperature, liquid loses heat continuously to the surroundings until it attains the equilibrium. The amount of heat lost by the liquid depends on different factors like nature of liquid, nature of solid vessel, surface area of liquid exposed to the surroundings, temperature difference of liquid and its surroundings, etc. The loss of heat by different processes may be explained by different laws. If the temperature difference is maintained suitable (less than 35C) and all other factors which affect the amount of heat lost are made constant then, cooling of liquid follows the Newton’s law of cooling.
